summary.approach: Implemented a source-first reduced mechanical ornithopter using the supplied engineering completion where the notebook leaves numbers, coefficients or detailed link geometry unspecified.

derived_from_photo_02.notes: Used the rounded 'Say' full span 7.4 ft and wrist span 3.7 ft = 50% of full span. Excluded the inconsistent 3.135 ft wing-length conversion as directed. Area comes from 14^2 / AR for the 14 m engineering span.

Wrist span 3.7 ft = 50% b
Area paragraph states AR = 8.29 from the scaled planform estimate

Exact outline between measured stations is inferred from the swan drawing plus supplied source mechanism geometry

readable_details: The chart shows low-Re curved-plate trends with ambiguous exact values
uncertain_or_rejected: Did not digitise exact CL/CD tables from the photograph
Did not claim these curves are full-scale swan coefficients

selected_photographs.principle_used: Human-carrying ornithopter intent and the sine-wave target-trajectory / required-force method.
readable_details: Defines an ideal trajectory as a sine wave
States candidate wing actions should be judged against the required wing forces
Explicitly frames the problem as a powered man-carrying ornithopter
uncertain_or_rejected: No engine, mass budget or numerical drive model is specified on this page
selected_photographs.engineering_completion_used: Used the supplied 16 kW engine, mass budget and reduced strip model while preserving the source force-matching idea.

selected_photographs.principle_used: Straight-and-level flapping requires cyclic lift and thrust variation rather than perfectly steady forces.
readable_details: Progress follows an undulating trajectory at slightly unsteady airspeed
Ring-gait wake context
uncertain_or_rejected: No exact powered aircraft mechanism is specified
selected_photographs.engineering_completion_used: Simulation keeps real cyclic force variation from the moving wing rather than prescribing fixed steady lift.

selected_photographs.principle_used: Low-speed downstroke lasts longer than recovery; cruising tends toward equal timing; wing-body resonance reduces inertial power.
readable_details: Low speed: longer flap-down duration
Cruise: periods become equal
Candidate wing actions should be matched to required lift and drag
uncertain_or_rejected: Handwritten marginal revisions are not fully legible
selected_photographs.engineering_completion_used: Used theta = phi - b sin(phi) with low-speed bias b=0.3 and cruise b=0, plus the supplied coupled spring/inertia model.

selected_photographs.principle_used: Wing/body mass-spring resonance, fore-aft wing motion, pitching reaction, and force directions from actual wing motion.
readable_details: Wing and body inertias with wishbone spring resonate at flapping frequency
Fore and aft movement changes cg-to-lift separation and introduces pitching moment
Outer hand wing trails on recovery
uncertain_or_rejected: Magnitude of the superimposed wing/body resonance effect is discussed qualitatively
selected_photographs.engineering_completion_used: Used source-mechanism mass derivatives, real moving application-point velocities, sweep linkage, and coupled phase/pitch equations.

selected_photographs.principle_used: Continuation of wing-action argument; incidence and camber are distinct; different bird examples share basic parts but not the same exact proportions.
readable_details: Incidences are adjusted to optimise thrust and drag
Goshawk drawing is an example of wing parts and section variation
uncertain_or_rejected: The goshawk camber percentages are not treated as swan specifications
selected_photographs.engineering_completion_used: Implemented independent twist/incidence and camber phase curves rather than conflating them.

selected_photographs.principle_used: Arm wing about 5-6% thick; outer hand wing effectively a thin curved/slotted plate; recovery partly closes the outer wing; conventional tail/rudder are acceptable.
readable_details: Arm thickness 5 to 6%
Outer hand wing negligible thickness
Trailing and partial closing on recovery reduces tip area and drag
Tail or weight-shift controls are compatible
uncertain_or_rejected: No exact mechanical tail geometry is given
selected_photographs.engineering_completion_used: Used supplied thickness fractions, two overlapping sliding outer leaves, recovery exposure reduction, and a conventional tail/fin/rudder mechanical completion.

selected_photographs.principle_used: Glide power as baseline and powered-flight power as the sum of extra aerodynamic, trajectory and inertial terms; spring transfers energy but does not create net propulsion energy.
readable_details: Base line power from gliding drag times speed
Additional powered terms include induced/thrust effects, cyclic acceleration and wing inertia
Inertial power can vanish if damping is zero
uncertain_or_rejected: No complete numeric powered aircraft efficiency budget is present on the photographed page
selected_photographs.engineering_completion_used: Implemented real shaft work, aerodynamic dissipation, transmission/damping heat, and finite fuel burn; the spring only stores and returns mechanical energy.

visual_and_mechanical_completion.description: The rendered aircraft is an engineered swan-derived ornithopter with broad inner wings, tapered rounded outer leaves, exposed transmission, trussed fuselage, seated pilot, three wheels, and conventional tail/rudder surfaces.
assumptions_not_claimed_as_stanley: 16 kW engine selection and governor model
Transmission efficiency, equivalent inertia and BSFC
Mass allocations except pilot and engine reference
Specific tail area, arm, control torques and damping values

limitations: The notebook photographs do not supply a full validated ornithopter design; the submission uses the provided reduced engineering completion wherever the handwriting does not fix a number.
The aerodynamic model omits wake history, hysteresis, section pitching moment and overlap-flow interaction.
The visual design is a plausible mechanical completion within the provided lightweight renderer, not a reconstructed historic build.
